holder.title: Hölder's inequality
holder.body: In mathematical analysis, Hölder's inequality, named after Otto Hölder, is a fundamental inequality between integrals and an indispensable tool for the study of Lp spaces.

holder.title: Hölder's inequality
holder.body:
Let (X, Sigma, mu) be any measure space and 1 <= p, q <= infinity with 1/p + 1/q = 1 (1/infinity = 0). For all measurable f, g: X -> C, ||fg||_1 <= ||f||_p ||g||_q (with the convention 0 * infinity = 0; so if f in L^p and g in L^q then fg in L^1 and |int fg dmu| <= ||f||_p ||g||_q). Equality case, 1 < p < infinity and ||f||_p, ||g||_q finite: ||fg||_1 = ||f||_p ||g||_q if and only if there are constants alpha, beta >= 0, not both zero, with alpha |f|^p = beta |g|^q mu-a.e. Generalized form: if 0 < p_1, ..., p_k <= infinity and 0 < r with 1/r = 1/p_1 + ... + 1/p_k, then ||f_1 ... f_k||_r <= ||f_1||_{p_1} ... ||f_k||_{p_k} (valid also for r < 1, by applying the two-factor case to |f_i|^r). Duality formula, with the semifiniteness caveat: for 1 <= p < infinity and f in L^p(mu), ||f||_p = sup{ |int fg dmu| : ||g||_{p'} <= 1 } over an ARBITRARY measure space; for measurable f with ||f||_p = infinity (1 < p < infinity), and for p = infinity, the identity requires mu to be SEMIFINITE. Counterexample without semifiniteness: X = {pt} with mu({pt}) = infinity; every g with ||g||_{p'} <= 1 and p' < infinity vanishes, so the supremum is 0, while for f = 1 one has ||f||_p = infinity for 1 < p < infinity and ||f||_infinity = 1.
(X, Sigma, mu) is a measure space (no finiteness needed for the inequality itself)
f and g are Sigma-measurable
1 <= p, q <= infinity and 1/p + 1/q = 1
convention 0 * infinity = 0
for the equality characterization: 1 < p < infinity and both norms finite
for the duality formula: either f in L^p with p < infinity, or mu semifinite

holder.title: Holder's inequality
holder.body: Let (X, Sigma, mu) be a measure space and let p, q in [1, infinity] be conjugate exponents, meaning 1/p + 1/q = 1 (with 1/infinity read as 0). If f is in L^p(mu) and g is in L^q(mu), then fg is in L^1(mu) and integral of |fg| dmu <= ||f||_p ||g||_q, where ||f||_p = (integral |f|^p dmu)^(1/p) for p < infinity and the essential supremum of |f| for p = infinity. The discrete form is sum |x_i y_i| <= (sum |x_i|^p)^(1/p) (sum |y_i|^q)^(1/q). For 1 < p < infinity, equality holds iff |f|^p and |g|^q are proportional a.e.

markov.title: Markov's inequality
markov.body: In probability theory, Markov's inequality gives an upper bound on the probability that a non-negative random variable is greater than or equal to some positive constant. Markov's inequality is tight in the sense that for each chosen positive constant, there exists a random variable such that the inequality is in fact an equality.

markov.title: Markov's Inequality
markov.body:
Let X be a nonnegative random variable (or f a nonnegative measurable function on a measure space, integrated against the measure) and a > 0. Then P(X >= a) <= E[X] / a. More generally, if phi: [0, infinity) -> [0, infinity) is nondecreasing and phi(a) > 0, then for any real random variable X, P(X >= a) <= E[phi(X^+)] / phi(a), and for any X and a > 0, P(|X| >= a) <= E|X|^p / a^p for every p > 0 (Markov applied to |X|^p). The bound is attained: for X taking the value a with probability m/a and 0 otherwise (0 < m <= a), E X = m and P(X >= a) = m/a.
X >= 0 almost surely for the basic form (no moment assumption beyond E X, which may be infinite - then the bound is trivial)
a > 0
phi nondecreasing with phi(a) > 0 in the general form

markov.title: Markov's Inequality
markov.body:
Let X be an almost surely non-negative random variable, and let t > 0. Then P(X >= t) <= E[X] / t.
X >= 0 almost surely
t > 0

hoeffding.title: Hoeffding's Inequality
hoeffding.body:
Let X_1, ..., X_n be independent random variables with X_i taking values in [a_i, b_i], and let S = sum X_i. Then for all t > 0, P(S - ES >= t) <= exp(-2 t^2 / sum (b_i - a_i)^2), and the same bound holds for the lower tail; hence a two-sided bound with a factor 2.
X_i independent
X_i in [a_i, b_i] almost surely

hoeffding.title: Hoeffding's inequality
hoeffding.body: In probability theory, Hoeffding's inequality provides an upper bound on the probability that the sum of bounded independent random variables deviates from its expected value by more than a certain amount. Hoeffding's inequality was proven by Wassily Hoeffding in 1963.

hoeffding.title: Azuma-Hoeffding Inequality
hoeffding.body:
Let (M_k) be a martingale (or supermartingale for the upper tail) with respect to a filtration, with bounded increments |M_k - M_{k-1}| <= c_k almost surely. Then for all t > 0, P(M_n - M_0 >= t) <= exp(-t^2 / (2 sum of c_k^2)), and symmetrically for the lower tail: martingales with bounded steps concentrate like sums of independent bounded variables.
(M_k) a martingale for the given filtration
increments bounded: |M_k - M_{k-1}| <= c_k a.s.

slutsky.title: Slutsky's theorem
slutsky.body: In probability theory, Slutsky's theorem extends some properties of algebraic operations on convergent sequences of real numbers to sequences of random variables.

slutsky.title: Slutsky's theorem
slutsky.body: Let X_n, X be random variables or vectors with X_n -> X in distribution as n -> infinity, and let Y_n -> c in probability for a constant c. Then X_n + Y_n -> X + c in distribution, X_n Y_n -> c X in distribution, and, provided c is not 0, X_n / Y_n -> X / c in distribution. More generally, if g(x,y) is continuous at every point (x,c), then g(X_n,Y_n) -> g(X,c) in distribution. Slutsky's theorem lets one combine a distributional limit with a probability limit as though the latter were a genuine constant. Due to Eugen Slutsky.

slutsky.title: Slutsky's Theorem (and Why the Second Limit Must Be Constant)
slutsky.body:
Let X_n converge in distribution to X and let Y_n converge in probability to a CONSTANT c. Then (X_n, Y_n) converges in distribution to (X, c) jointly, and consequently X_n + Y_n converges in distribution to X + c, X_n Y_n converges in distribution to cX, and if c is not 0 then X_n / Y_n converges in distribution to X / c. The constancy of the limit of Y_n is essential and is not a technical convenience: convergence in distribution alone gives no information about joint behaviour. Take X symmetric with X_n = X for all n and Y_n = -X for all n; then X_n converges in distribution to X and Y_n converges in distribution to X by symmetry, yet X_n + Y_n = 0 does not converge in distribution to X + X = 2X unless X is degenerate. Likewise convergence in probability of Y_n cannot be weakened to convergence in distribution even when the limit is constant, because for a constant limit those two modes coincide, which is precisely why the theorem can be stated with either for a constant target. [standard; e.g. van der Vaart, Asymptotic Statistics, Theorem 2.8]
X_n => X in distribution
Y_n -> c in probability with c a CONSTANT (not a random variable)
for the quotient: c != 0
